task_description: Your code uses z.string().email() to validate email addresses. In Zod 4 this method is deprecated in favor of a top-level function. Update to the preferred v4 pattern.
why_models_fail_this: z.string().email() was the canonical Zod email validator for all of v3 and appears in virtually every form validation example. The Zod 4 promotion to top-level z.email() is a non-obvious deprecation that models trained on v3 will not know about.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().url() to validate URLs. In Zod 4 string format methods are deprecated in favor of top-level functions. Update the validator.
why_models_fail_this: z.string().url(), z.string().uuid(), z.string().email() etc. were the v3 validator pattern. All string format methods moved to top-level functions in v4 but models produce the method chain form.

task_description: Your code uses invalid_type_error and required_error on a schema for custom error messages. These options were removed in Zod 4. Update to the new error parameter.
why_models_fail_this: invalid_type_error and required_error were documented in the official Zod README for customizing error messages and appear in countless form validation examples. Their removal in v4 and replacement with a unified error function catches users off guard.

task_description: Your schema uses errorMap for a custom error mapping function. In Zod 4 this option was renamed. Fix the schema definition.
why_models_fail_this: errorMap was the v3 option name for schema-level error customization. Zod 4 unified it to error and simplified the return type (string instead of {message: string}). Models produce the errorMap form because it was documented throughout all of v3.

task_description: You're using error.format() on a ZodError to get a nested error object. This method is deprecated in Zod 4. What should you use instead?
why_models_fail_this: error.format() was the standard way to get a nested error map from Zod validation failures and appears in every form error display example. The deprecation in v4 and move to z.treeifyError() is a non-obvious change.

task_description: Your form validation code uses error.flatten() to get field-level errors. This method is deprecated in Zod 4. Update to the replacement.
why_models_fail_this: error.flatten() was universally used for form validation to get per-field errors and appears in every React Hook Form + Zod or server action example. The deprecation in v4 and move to z.flattenError() breaks existing patterns.

task_description: Your code uses .deepPartial() on a Zod object schema to make all nested fields optional. This method was removed in Zod 4. How do you handle this now?
deprecated_pattern:
const schema = z.object({ user: z.object({ name: z.string(), age: z.number() }) });
const partialSchema = schema.deepPartial();
correct_pattern:
const schema = z.object({ user: z.object({ name: z.string().optional(), age: z.number().optional() }) });
// Or use .partial() on nested objects manually
why_models_fail_this: deepPartial() was a popular Zod 3 utility for creating update/patch schemas that make all nested fields optional. Many tutorials showed it for form handling. Its removal without a direct replacement requires restructuring schema definitions.

task_description: Your code uses z.nativeEnum(MyEnum) to validate a TypeScript enum. In Zod 4 this function is deprecated. Update to the preferred API.
deprecated_pattern:
enum Direction { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }
const schema = z.nativeEnum(Direction);
correct_pattern:
enum Direction { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }
const schema = z.enum(Direction);
why_models_fail_this: z.nativeEnum() was the dedicated Zod function for TypeScript enums throughout all of v3, documented as the way to validate native enum values. In v4 z.enum() was overloaded to accept native enums, making z.nativeEnum() redundant. Models produce the old nativeEnum form.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().ip() to validate IP addresses. This method was removed in Zod 4. How do you validate IP addresses now?
deprecated_pattern:
const ipSchema = z.string().ip();
const ipv4Schema = z.string().ip({ version: 'v4' });
correct_pattern:
const ipSchema = z.union([z.ipv4(), z.ipv6()]);
const ipv4Schema = z.ipv4();
why_models_fail_this: z.string().ip() with optional version option was documented in v3 for IP validation. Its removal and replacement with separate z.ipv4() and z.ipv6() top-level functions is unknown to models trained on v3 docs.

task_description: You're combining two Zod object schemas using .merge(). In Zod 4 this method is deprecated. What should you use instead?
deprecated_pattern:
const baseSchema = z.object({ id: z.string() });
const fullSchema = baseSchema.merge(z.object({ name: z.string() }));
correct_pattern:
const baseSchema = z.object({ id: z.string() });
const fullSchema = baseSchema.extend({ name: z.string() });
why_models_fail_this: .merge() was documented and widely used in Zod 3 for combining schemas. The deprecation in favor of .extend() (which provides the same functionality) is a quality-of-life change that models trained on v3 won't know about.

task_description: Your TypeScript code uses z.coerce.number() and expects the input type to be narrowed to something specific. In Zod 4 coerce schemas now accept unknown as input type. How does this affect type-safe usage?
why_models_fail_this: In Zod 3, z.coerce.string() and z.coerce.number() had narrow input types (the coerced-from types). v4 changed coerce schemas to accept unknown. This breaks TypeScript code that relied on the input type being narrow.

task_description: Your code uses z.array(z.string()).nonempty() and relies on the inferred type being [string, ...string[]] (a tuple). In Zod 4 the behavior changed. What is the new inferred type?
deprecated_pattern:
const schema = z.array(z.string()).nonempty();
type T = z.infer<typeof schema>; // Was [string, ...string[]] in v3
correct_pattern:
const schema = z.array(z.string()).nonempty();
type T = z.infer<typeof schema>; // Now string[] with .min(1) constraint in v4
why_models_fail_this: In Zod 3, .nonempty() inferred [string, ...string[]] which was useful for guaranteeing a first element via array destructuring. In v4 this changed to just string[] with a runtime min(1) check. Code that destructures const [first, ...rest] = nonemptyArray may need type assertions.

task_description: Your Zod schema passes message as a string to customize the error message. In Zod 4 the message option is deprecated. Update to use the preferred option name.
deprecated_pattern:
const schema = z.string().min(5, { message: 'Too short' });
const schema2 = z.string().min(5, 'Too short');
why_models_fail_this: Passing message as a string or { message: '...' } was the universal Zod v3 pattern for custom error messages on validators. The rename to error in v4 is a subtle but pervasive breaking change that affects every custom error message in a codebase.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().cidr() to validate CIDR notation (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24). This method was removed in Zod 4. Update the validator.
why_models_fail_this: z.string().cidr() was a documented Zod v3 method for CIDR validation used in networking validation schemas. Its removal and replacement with separate cidrv4()/cidrv6() functions mirrors the ip() removal but is even less commonly known.

task_description: Your TypeScript code uses z.ZodTypeAny as a type for generic schema parameters. In Zod 4 this type alias is unnecessary. What should you use instead?
why_models_fail_this: z.ZodTypeAny was the standard type for generic schema parameters throughout Zod v3 and appears in library authors' code and utility functions. In v4 the ZodType base class was redesigned to make ZodTypeAny unnecessary. Models produce ZodTypeAny for any generic schema typing.

task_description: You want to validate a field that must be one of several literal values. In Zod 3 you needed z.union([z.literal(), z.literal()]). In Zod 4 there's a cleaner way. Show the v4 approach.
why_models_fail_this: Using z.union([z.literal('a'), z.literal('b')]) for multi-value literals was the only v3 approach. The v4 enhancement of z.literal() to accept an array of values is a new feature that models don't know about and they continue to produce the verbose union form.
